claims.text: Under sustained creep loading at controlled temperature, progressive plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayers is governed primarily by dislocations nucleated at nanoscale interfaces.
The nanoscale interfaces exhibit severe lattice distortion.
The nanoscale interfaces possess intrinsic short-range order.
Severe lattice distortion and short-range order at the interfaces promote localized atomic diffusion.
Localized interfacial diffusion promotes the formation of dislocation channels.
The formation of dislocation channels gradually accelerates creep relative to the as-deposited state.
The initial as-deposited coatings have nanoscale layer thicknesses and coherent interfaces.
The initial as-deposited coatings have minimal pre-existing dislocation density.
Distorted interfaces act as preferential sites for dislocation nucleation under sustained loading.
Local lattice distortion and short-range order enhance atomic mobility.
Enhanced atomic mobility facilitates the propagation of dislocation channels.
Interface-mediated dislocation-channel formation produces progressive plastic deformation.
Sustained loading will increase the density of dislocation channels localized at interfaces relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Sustained loading will enhance interfacial atomic diffusion relative to the as-deposited baseline.
The creep strain rate will accelerate over time.
The proposed mechanism dominates only while the nanoscale multilayer structure and its interfaces remain intact.
The proposed mechanism applies at stresses that activate dislocation processes without causing catastrophic failure.
There is converging evidence that interface-mediated dislocation accumulation drives accelerated creep.
The relative contributions of enhanced interfacial diffusion and strain-induced short-range-order evolution are not yet precisely quantified.
Failure to observe increased interface-specific dislocation accumulation or changed interfacial diffusion together with the predicted creep behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
